Consult Summary:
- 50-year-old female with 6 days of dysuria, malodorous urine, intermittent midline lower abdominal pain and visible blood spots in urine. 
- Clinician treated presumptive lower urinary tract infection with a 3-day course of antibiotics (prescription sent to patient-selected pharmacy) and provided supportive advice; advised return if symptoms worsen or recur.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Acute dysuria with hematuria and lower abdominal pain (presumptive urinary tract infection)
- Presentation: 6 days of painful and malodorous urination, intermittent midline lower abdominal pain (pain rated 7/10), and spotting of blood in urine. First occurrence.
- Review of systems / pertinent negatives: No fever reported, no loin or lower back pain, no vaginal discharge, eating/drinking OK, no change in bowel habit, no weight loss.
- Social factors: Lives with friends; no recent dehydration or increased sexual activity reported.
- Examination findings: No physical examination findings documented.
- Diagnostic testing: No urine dipstick or culture documented; patient does not have a thermometer at time of consult (advised to obtain one).
- Assessment / differential: Clinician impression — likely lower urinary tract infection (cystitis).
- Management given: Empiric antibiotics prescribed for 3 days (medication name/dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript). Prescription sent to Knightsbridge Practice pharmacy. Advice to drink 2.5–3.0 L fluid per day, consider cranberry juice and over-the-counter urinary acidity sachets. Monitor temperature; obtain a thermometer. Return/seek urgent review if pain worsens, develops fever, develops lower back/loin pain, cannot pass urine, or symptoms do not resolve or recur.

Issue 2: Irritable bowel syndrome (past medical history)
- History: Patient reports prior diagnosis of IBS. No recent change in bowel habit and no rectal bleeding reported at this visit.
- Medications: Takes mebeverine regularly.
- Assessment / management: No active management changes discussed.

Issue 3: Drug allergy — clindamycin
- Patient-reported allergy to clindamycin. No reaction details documented.
- Management: Allergy documented; avoid clindamycin.

Medications:
- Mebeverine 200 mg three times daily (patient-stated).
- Antibiotics prescribed for presumed UTI — specific agent and dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
- Clindamycin (reaction details not documented).

Past Medical History:
- Irritable bowel syndrome.
- No other medical problems or prior surgeries reported.

Social History:
- Lives with friends.
- Occupation: Support worker.
- Alcohol: Occasional; approximately one glass of wine per week.
- Tobacco: Non-smoker.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, bone density, vaccinations, recent optometry or skin checks) documented in the transcript.

Physical Examination:
- No vitals documented.
- No physical exam documented.

Plan:
- Pharmacy: Send antibiotic prescription to Knightsbridge Practice pharmacy (done during consult); patient to pick up and start immediately.
- Self-care: Increase oral fluids to 2.5–3.0 L/day; consider cranberry juice and OTC urinary acidity sachets.
- Monitoring: Patient to obtain a thermometer and check temperature regularly.
- Escalation instructions: Return or seek urgent care if fever develops, lower back/loin pain occurs, inability to void, worsening pain, or if symptoms do not improve after treatment or recur.
- Follow-up: No routine follow-up arranged if symptoms resolve; review if symptoms persist or recur.

Quality checks / Document quality:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (temperature), urine dipstick and/or urine culture, pregnancy status/last menstrual details relevant to hematuria and antibiotic choice, specific antibiotic name/dose/route/frequency, details of any allergic reaction to clindamycin, focused abdominal and pelvic examination findings.
- Internal conflicts from transcript: None identified.
- Transcript quality comment: Overall intelligible with occasional brief inaudible segments and repetition; clinical content sufficient to document presenting complaint, history, and plan.
